titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — Epilogue II: the blessing and the first curses (xli 75 – xlii 97)
part: Epilogue II · the blessing and the first curses (Col. xli 75 – xlii 97)
about: The second part of the epilogue, in which the king turns from the charge to later kings to the reward and the punishment: first a long blessing for the man who respects the stele, then the first curses on the man who does not. The blessing opens with a “whoever” in the style of the laws: if that man has good judgment and can guide his land aright, let him heed the words written on the stele, let the stele show him the way, the guidance, the verdicts and the rulings, let him guide the black-headed people, judge their cases, root out the wicked and the evil, and bring his people well-being (xli 75–94). Hammurabi names himself, king of justice, to whom Shamash gave truths; his words are weighty and his deeds have no rival (xli 95–102). A stretch follows that I cannot read (xli 103 – xlii 1). Then the blessing proper: if that man has heeded the words and has not effaced, overruled or changed the king’s verdict, words and designs, then he, a king of justice like Hammurabi, is wished a long scepter and a people shepherded in justice (xlii 2–17). The first curse begins at xlii 18: the man who ignores the words, forgets the curses, fears not the curse of the gods, blots out the king’s verdicts and designs, erases the inscribed name and writes his own, or has someone else do it — whether king, lord, governor or any person with a name — is cursed in turn by three deities: the great god, father of the gods, is asked to turn the glory of kingship away from him, to break his scepter and to curse his fates (xlii 39–52); Ellil, the lord who fixes the fates, is to decree for him a reign of sighing, few days, years of famine, darkness without light and sudden death, and to pronounce the ruin of his city, the scattering of his people and the loss of his name (xlii 53–80); and Bēlit, the great mother, is to turn his word to evil before Ellil, and to have the overthrow of his land and the pouring out of his life like water set on him (xlii 81–97). The numbers in the margin are the stele’s own line numbers, not law numbers. Several readings are uncertain, and the notes say where: the unread lines at xli 103–105, the verb uštepiel, the name of the god at xlii 45, the stretch xlii 59–63, the words šūbilam and igirrû, and the reading of the goddess’s name (Harper’s Bēlit, written NIN.LÍL). In xlii 5–9 Harper’s print has one divider too few; the plate and his own glossary show that a-wa-ti-ia (7), la uš-te-pi-el (8) and u-zu-ra-ti-ia (9) are three separate lines.

sentences.l: If that-man discernment has-and, his-land to-guide-aright is-able,
sentences.i: If that man has discernment and is able to guide his land aright,
sentences.n: A new part of the epilogue begins, and it turns to blessing: a long “if”, whose good result the king then spells out. Read it like the laws’ šumma-clauses: šumma awīlum šū is “if that man” (šū after the noun is “that one, the man in question”), followed by the conditions. tašīmtam īšuma is tašīmtum “discernment, good judgment” (Harper’s tasimtu, “wisdom, diplomacy”) + īšu “he has” (išûm) + -ma “and”, which ties this clause to the next. mātassu is mātum “land” + -šu “his”: the t of the noun and the š of the suffix are said ss and written with the ZU sign (Harper’s ma-zu), the way šarrūssu is written in xlii 75. šutēšuram is the Št infinitive of ešērum “to be straight” (Harper’s “to rule with right”) in the accusative, “to guide aright”; ileʾʾi “he is able” (leʾûm; Harper’s i-li-i) comes last, as the verb does.

sentences.l: to the-words which on my-stele I-wrote let-him-heed, and
sentences.i: let him pay heed to the words that I wrote on my stele, and
sentences.n: The result of the blessing begins: “then let him …”. ana awâtim is “to the words” (awâtim, the plural of awātum in the genitive after ana); ša ina narûya ašṭuru is a relative clause, “which on my stele I wrote”, with its verb last and in the subjunctive (-u), as in xli 62. liqūlma is li- (“let him”) + qūl + -ma, the precative of qâlum “to heed”. Harper files li-gul-ma and the later i-gul-ma (xlii 5, 22) under QALU, “to give attention to”, so I normalize the verb as qâlum; the sign he reads gul is kept as he writes it in the reading line. The root and the vowels are not settled, and the sense is Harper’s: UNCERTAIN. The -ma joins this clause to the next two units.

sentences.l: the-way, the-guidance, the-case of-the-land which I-judged, the-decisions of-the-land which I-decided,
sentences.i: the way, the guidance, the verdicts that I gave for the land, the rulings that I decided for the land,
sentences.n: Four things are listed one after another with no “and”; the verb that governs them is likallimšuma in the next unit (“let that stele show him …”). kibsam is kibsum “tread, way, procedure” (Harper’s kibsu, from kabāsum “to tread”); rīdam is “guidance, leadership”, as in xl 6. dīn mātim ša adīnu and purussê mātim ša aprusu are the two clauses of xli 68: “the verdict of the land that I judged, the decision of the land that I decided”. mâtim is written with the sign KALAM “land” (Harper’s circumflex marks a Sumerogram), read mātim. adīnu: Harper files a-di-nu under dânum “to judge, to decide” (his danu I,1, with i-di-in in §6 and li-di-in at xli 88); his glossary lists this very word, a-di-nu, at xli 69 (the parallel line in the part before), at xli 81 and at xlii 27, all under that verb. dīn adīnu is then “the verdict I judged”, a verb and its own noun, as dīnam idīn in §5. The part before (epilogue-1, xli 68) took the same word as addinu, nadānum “I gave”; one d cannot settle that, but Harper’s grouping and the paired noun and verb favour dânum, so it is read the same way in all three places here. Both readings make a verdict, so the English is the same, “the verdicts that I gave”.

sentences.l: the-stele that let-it-show-him-and,
sentences.i: let that stele show them to him, and
sentences.n: The subject of the wish at last: narûm šū “that stele” (šū again “that one”). likallimšuma is li- + kallim, the precative of the D-stem of kalāmum “to show” (as at xli 12), + -šu “to him” + -ma “and”: “let it show him”. What the stele is to show was listed in the unit before (the way, the guidance, the verdicts, the rulings). The “and” leads to the next two wishes, which say what the man himself is to do.

sentences.l: the-black-ones of-his-head let-him-guide-aright,
sentences.i: let him guide his black-headed people aright,
sentences.n: ṣalmāt qaqqadišu is the phrase of the prologue, here spelt out in syllables: ṣalmāt, the plural of ṣalmum “black” (Harper’s “black, Black-Head race, i.e. mankind”), + qaqqadišu “his head” (qaqqadum + -šu), the house rendering being “the black-headed people”; here they are the people of the man who obeys the stele. lištēšir is li- + the Št preterite of ešērum “to be straight”: the same verb as šutēšuram in xli 77 (Harper’s III,2), “let him guide aright”. (Harper’s ga-ga-di-šu; the GA sign is read qa₂.)

sentences.l: their-case let-him-judge, their-decision let-him-decide.
sentences.i: let him judge their case, let him decide their decision.
sentences.n: Two matching wishes, each with its verb last and made from the same root as its object. dīnšina lidīn: dīnum “case, verdict” + -šina “their” (the black-headed people’s), and lidīn is li- + idīn, the preterite of dânum “to judge” (Harper’s danu; the same verb as idīn in §5): “let him judge their case”. purussâšina liprus: purussûm “decision”, accusative singular before a suffix (purussâ-, as purussâm in §6; Harper’s glossary lists pu-ru-za-ši-na next to pu-ru-za-am), with the double s written with ZA, + -šina “their”; liprus is li- + iprus, parāsum “to decide”: “let him decide their decision”, the noun and the verb of one root, as dīnšina lidīn above.

sentences.l: in his-land the-wicked and the-evil let-him-uproot,
sentences.i: let him uproot the wicked and the evil one from his land,
sentences.n: ina mātišu “in his land” (mātum + -šu) opens the next wish; raggam u ṣēnam “the wicked and the evil one” are accusatives, the same pair as in the prologue (ra-ga-am u ṣi-nam), and u “and” is written with the sign ù (U3), as in epilogue-1. li-zu-uḫ is Harper’s lizzuḫ, the doubled consonant being written with ZU: li- + nasāḫum “to pluck out, to uproot” (Harper’s nasahu I,1, with li-iz-zu-uḫ-šu at xliii 36), the precative with the n assimilated: lissuḫ, “let him uproot”.

sentences.l: the-flesh of-his-people let-him-make-good.
sentences.i: and let him bring well-being to his people.
sentences.n: šīr nišīšu liṭīb: šīrum “flesh, well-being” (Harper’s siru, “flesh, well-being”), nišīšu “his people” (nišū + -šu, as in the prologue), and liṭīb the precative of the D-stem of ṭâbum “to be good” (Harper’s tabu II,1, “to benefit, to content”; compare uṭīb in the litany): literally “let him make good the flesh of his people”, that is, let him bring them well-being. This ends the list of wishes for the man who heeds the stele.

sentences.l: Hammurabi, king of-justice, to-whom Shamash truths gave, I(-am).
sentences.i: I am Hammurabi, the king of justice, to whom Shamash gave truths.
sentences.n: The king speaks of himself again, in a nominal sentence with anāku “I (am)” at the end, as at xl 10. Ḫammurabi šar mīšarim is “Hammurabi, king of justice” (the sign LUGAL read šar, “king of”, with mīšarim “of justice”, the title of xl 75 and xli 7). ša Šamaš kīnātim išrukušum is a relative clause with the verb in the subjunctive: “to whom Shamash gave truths”. išrukušum is išruk (the preterite of šarākum “to give”) + the subjunctive -u + -šum “to him”, the -u short before -šum, and the -šum looks back to Hammurabi: “the one to whom Shamash gave”. kīnātim is the plural of kittum “truth” (the litany’s lemma; kīnātum is the plural of kittum, from the root of kīnum “firm”; Harper lists ki-na-tim under his kinatu “justice”). The plate (Plate 76, row 97) shows the god’s star before UTU; Harper writes his name Šamaš.

sentences.l: my-words weighty(-are); my-deeds a-rival not have.
sentences.i: My words are weighty; my deeds have no rival.
sentences.n: Two short clauses, as at xl 79–80. awâtūa našqā “my words (are) weighty”: našqā is the stative plural of našqum “weighty, choice” (Harper’s našku, with the GA sign read qa₂), agreeing with awâtūa “my words” (awātum + -ia, written u-a). ipšētūa šāninam ul īšā “my deeds have no rival”: ipšētum “deed” (Harper’s epištu) + -ia, šāninam “a rival” (šanānum “to rival”, Harper’s šananu; accusative), ul “not”, and īšā the 3rd plural feminine of išûm “to have”, agreeing with ipšētūa (the plural subject); at xl 80 the verb is īša after a singular subject.

sentences.l: except(?) to la-ḫa(?) ZI-IM.RI.GA(?); to im-ki-im(?)
sentences.i: Except [for la-ḫa ZI-IM.RI.GA, which I cannot read]; for the wise (?) …
sentences.n: This stretch I cannot read, and I read as little of it as the evidence allows. e-la carries a footnote in Harper’s print: “Peiser, e-la a-na la-ḫa-zi-im ri-qa”, that is, Peiser takes la-ḫa and the capital signs ZI-IM.RI.GA as la-ḫa-zi-im and ri-qa. e-la itself looks like ēla “except, apart from”, but that is a guess from the spelling. la-ḫa and ZI-IM.RI.GA Harper gives as bare signs (capitals, without a reading), which means he could not read them as words: I keep them unread. a-na is ana “to, for”. im-ki-im is entered in Harper’s glossary as IM-KI-IM (?), an unsettled word; as emqum is “wise”, imqim “of the wise one (?)” would fit the signs (KI read qi₂), but I keep Harper’s spelling and mark the reading uncertain. On the plate (Plate 76) line 103 is e-la a-na la-ḫa; lines 104 and 105 stand in one ruled box with two half-height rows (ZI-IM.RI.GA above, a-na im-ki-im below). Harper’s own numerals agree with taking them as two lines: his print puts the numeral 105 at a-na im-ki-im, straight after ZI-IM.RI.GA (so ZI-IM.RI.GA is 104), and the column ends there.

sentences.l: for might(?) brought-out(?).
sentences.i: …, for might (?), brought out (?).
sentences.n: These two words end the stretch begun at xli 103 and are as uncertain as it. ana tanādātim: Harper’s glossary has tanatu “might, tyranny” for ta-na-da-tim (the d spelled for t); I keep “might” and mark it uncertain. (From memory of the standard lexicon, not checked here: later dictionaries read the word as tanādātim, the plural of tanittum “praise, glory”; Harper’s “might, tyranny” is his own reading and stays the base.) šuṣâ is entered by Harper under his wasu III,1, the Š-stem of waṣûm “to go out” (su-sa-a); the form (a stative plural? an imperative?) and the subject are not clear to me, and the unit has no clear subject of its own (the words and deeds of xli 99–100 are the only candidates). The sense “brought out” is the dictionary meaning of the Š-stem, not a reading of this line. The word ta-na-da-{b}tim is broken between two sub-rows of one ruled line on the plate (Plate 76, row 1).

sentences.l: If that-man to my-words which on my-stele I-wrote has-heeded-and,
sentences.i: If that man has paid heed to my words that I wrote on my stele, and
sentences.n: The blessing’s second, longer “if”: the same pattern as xli 75–79, now about the man who obeys. a-na a-wa-ti-ia is “to my words” (awâtīya, awātum + -ia); ša ina narûya ašṭuru is the relative clause of xli 79, with the verb last and in the subjunctive; iqūlma is the preterite of qâlum “to heed” (Harper’s i-gul at xlii 5 and 22, the same verb as liqūlma at xli 79) + -ma “and”. This is a condition: the “if” clause runs on through the next unit, and the result comes at xlii 11.

sentences.l: my-verdict not he-has-effaced, my-words not he-has-overruled, my-designs not he-has-changed,
sentences.i: has not effaced my verdict, has not overruled my words, has not changed my designs,
sentences.n: The condition goes on with three negative verbs, each with lā: dīnī lā ušazziq, awâtīya lā uštepiel, uṣurātīya lā unakkir. dīnī is dīnum “verdict” + -ī “my”. ušazziq is the Š preterite of nazāqum (Harper’s “to efface, destroy”, as in ay ušazziq, xli 73). uštepiel is Harper’s bêlu III,1 “to overrule”: a Š-stem of a verb whose root and vowels I cannot settle, so the sense “overrule, set aside” is Harper’s (UNCERTAIN; the same word returns at xlii 30). unakkir is the D preterite of nakārum “to change” (as at xli 72); uṣurātīya “my designs”, as xli 73. PLATE: in this stretch Harper’s print has one divider too few (five lines are numbered between 5 and 10 but only four pieces of text are printed between the dividers), and the signs are divided here as his print divides them: 6 di-ni la u-ša-az-zi-iq, 7 a-wa-ti-ia la uš-te-pi-el, 8 u-zu-ra-ti-ia, 10 la u-na-ki-ir. On Plate 76 the ruled rows are in fact five (6 di-ni la u-ša-az-zi-iq, 7 a-wa-ti-ia, 8 la uš-te-pi-el, 9 u-zu-ra-ti-ia, 10 la u-na-ki-ir): row 7 is the same row of signs as row 29, row 8 is row 30 with an extra sign (la) in front, and Harper’s own glossary cites uš-te-pi-el at xlii 8 and u-zu-ra-ti-ia at xlii 9. The line-break marks here keep Harper’s four-line division only because the text file this part is checked against carries it; on the stone a-wa-ti-ia stands alone on line 7, la uš-te-pi-el on line 8 and u-zu-ra-ti-ia on line 9.

sentences.l: that-man, like me king of-justice, Shamash his-scepter let-him-lengthen,
sentences.i: that man, a king of justice like me: may Shamash lengthen his scepter,
sentences.n: The result of the second “if”, a blessing: awīlum šū kīma jâti šar mīšarim, “that man, like me a king of justice” (kīma jâti “like me”, jâti the accusative “me”; LUGAL read šar, the king’s own title as at xli 96). It is a nominal phrase put before the wish, so the man is named first and then blessed. {d}UTU is Shamash; GIŠ.PA-šu is ḫaṭṭašu “his scepter”, as in the litany (Harper’s ḫaṭṭi-šu); lirrik is Harper’s li-ir-ri-ik, his arāku II,1 “to prolong”, the precative “let him lengthen”. (The code writes li- before the D and Š stems throughout this part — liṭīb, lilemmin, litēršu, lišaškin — so lirrik is read as Harper prints it.)

sentences.l: his-people in justice let-him-shepherd.
sentences.i: and may he shepherd his people in justice.
sentences.n: nišīšu ina mīšarim lirʾi: “his people, in justice, let him shepherd”. lirʾi (written li-ri) is li- + the preterite of rêʾûm “to pasture, to shepherd”, the verb behind rēʾûm “shepherd”: the king who is “shepherd” in the litany is wished to rule as one. Harper’s glossary files li-ri under ARU II,1 “to carry, to rule” (with li-ru-su at xliv 23); I read it as rêʾûm, which suits “shepherd his people” (UNCERTAIN). The subject is the obedient man.

sentences.l: If that-man — my-words which on my-stele I-wrote —
sentences.i: If that man — as to my words, which I wrote on my stele —
sentences.n: The first of the curses. It opens exactly like the second “if” at xlii 2–5, with the same words and the same relative clause (ša ina narûya ašṭuru, verb last), but this man is the one who disobeys. The sentence hangs in the air until the next unit, which gives the verbs: “… and has not heeded, and …”. The unit is a new paragraph because the curses begin here. On the plate the signs of xlii 19 (a-wa-ti-ia) are partly drawn in outline, that is, worn or broken on the stone; the reading is not in doubt, since the same words stand at xlii 3 and 29.

sentences.l: not has-heeded-and, my-curses has-forgotten-and, the-curse of-the-gods not has-feared-and,
sentences.i: has not heeded them, and has forgotten my curses, and has not feared the curse of the gods, and
sentences.n: The conditions of the curse, a chain of past-tense clauses each ended with -ma “and”. lā iqūlma is “and has not heeded” (qâlum, as xlii 5). irrītīya imēšma: irrītum “curse” (Harper’s irritu) + -ia, “my curses”, and imēš the preterite of mašûm “to forget” (Harper’s masu I,1, i-me-eš; the e is his normalization). irrīt ilī lā idūrma: irrīt is irrītum before a genitive (the long ī kept, as in kibīt), ilī is the plural “gods”, here written NI.NI (the two triangle signs; Harper’s glossary lists NI.NI under ilu, at xlii 25 and 46, and his List of Signs gives ili as NI.NI, no. 99), and idūr is the preterite of adārum “to fear”: “and has not feared the curse of the gods”.

sentences.l: the-verdict I-judged he-has-blotted-out, my-words he-has-overruled, my-designs he-has-changed,
sentences.i: has blotted out the verdict I gave, has overruled my words, has changed my designs,
sentences.n: Three charges with perfect verbs. dīn adīnu uptassis: dīn adīnu is the relative clause without ša, “the verdict I judged” (as at xli 81, with ša there), and uptassis is the D perfect of pasāsum “to blot out, to abolish” (Harper’s pasasu II,2; his up-ta-az-zi-is writes the double s with z). awâtīya uštepiel is “has overruled my words”: the same form as xlii 8, there with lā (Harper files both under bêlu III,1; the sense “overrule” is his, UNCERTAIN). uṣurātīya uttakkir “has changed my designs”: uttakkir is the D perfect of nakārum, the form that goes with unakkir (xlii 10).

sentences.l: my-name inscribed he-has-erased-and, his-name he-has-written-out; because-of those curses another-indeed he-has-made-take,
sentences.i: has erased my inscribed name and written out his own name; and because of those curses has made another one take (it) (?),
sentences.n: The last charges: the name on the stele. šumī šaṭram ipšiṭma: šumī is šumum “name” + -ī “my”, šaṭram the passive participle “written, inscribed” (as in xl), ipšiṭ the preterite of pašāṭum “to efface” (Harper’s pasatu I,1) + -ma. šumšu ištadar: “his own name he has written out”, ištadar being the perfect of sadārum “to write out” (Harper’s sadaru I,2; compare isaddar). aššum irrītim šināti is “because of these curses”: aššum “because of”, irrītim the genitive, šināti the feminine plural “these” (Harper’s šū, fem. šī, plur. fem. šināti). šaniamma uštaḫiz: šaniam “another one” + -ma, and uštaḫiz the Š perfect of aḫāzum “to take” (Harper’s ahazu III,2): “he has made another take (it)”. UNCERTAIN: the sense, that the man gets someone else to do the erasing so as to avoid the curses, is my reading of the clause, not Harper’s.

sentences.l: that-man, whether king or lord or governor or any-person who a-name is-called,
sentences.i: that man, whether king or lord or governor, or any person who is called by a name —
sentences.n: The curse names whom it reaches, to show that no one is outside it: awīlum šū lū šarrum lū bēlum lū patesi ù lū awīlūtum. lū … lū is “whether … or”; šarrum is the sign LUGAL, bēlum the sign EN “lord”; PA.TE.SI is the Sumerian title of a city ruler (Harper keeps it as pa-te-si, and his index lists PA.TE.SI at xlii 42); ù lū are two words, “and/or whether”, as in earlier parts, with awīlūtum “mankind, a person” (Harper’s awilutu “man, mankind”). ša šumam nabiat “who is called by a name”: nabiat is Harper’s nabû I,1 “to name, call”, in the stative, 3rd feminine (agreeing with awīlūtum). The accusative šumam after a passive is unusual, so the sense “who bears a name” is UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: the-god great, father of-the-gods, who-named my-reign, the-glory of-kingship let-him-turn-away from-him,
sentences.i: may the great god, the father of the gods, who named my reign, turn the glory of kingship away from him,
sentences.n: A god is called on to take the kingship from the man: ilum rabûm abu ilī nābû palêya, “the great god, father of the gods, who named my reign”. ilum is the AN sign alone (read DINGIR “god”), which Harper reads ilum and does not name; abu is abum “father”; ilī is again NI.NI, the plural “gods”; nābû is the participle of nabûm “to name” (Harper’s nabu I,1); palêya is palûm “reign” + -ia, the BAL sign (Harper’s sign list no. 7, palû). The god is not named in the line: the titles (“great god, father of the gods”) point to Anum, but that is my inference. melam šarrūtim “the glory of kingship”: ME.LAM is melammum, “the awe-inspiring radiance” of a god or king (Harper’s melammu “glory”). litēršu is Harper’s li-te-ir-šu, taru II,1 (D), li- + the D of târum + -šu “from him / to him”: the D means “to turn back, give back”, so “let him turn it away from him” is my reading of the wish (UNCERTAIN: “let him take back from him”).

sentences.l: his-scepter let-him-break, his-destinies let-him-curse.
sentences.i: may he break his scepter, may he curse his destinies.
sentences.n: Two more wishes of the same god. ḫaṭṭašu lišbir: GIŠ.PA-šu “his scepter” (as at xlii 14, where the same man was to have it lengthened) and lišbir, li- + išbir, šebērum “to break”. šīmātišu lirur: šīmātum, the plural of šīmtum “fate”, + -šu, and lirur is li- + irur, the precative of arārum “to curse” (Harper’s araru I,1, with li-ru-ur-šu at xliv 89). The scepter is the sign of rule; “curse his fates” asks that what the gods have fixed for him turn against him.

sentences.l: Ellil, the-lord, who-fixes the-fates, whose-command not is-altered, who-makes-great my-kingship,
sentences.i: Ellil, the lord, who fixes the fates, whose command is not changed, who makes my kingship great —
sentences.n: A second god is called, with his titles. Harper prints his name Bêl, “lord”, which is the sign group {d}EN.LÍL, as at xl 64 (the star, then EN and KID); I write Ellil, as in epilogue-1, and bēlum “the lord” follows in syllables. Harper’s own glossary has BEL [EN.LIL], god, whose chief seat of worship was Nippur, at xlii 53, 89 and 95, and his List of Signs (no. 49) shows the group star + EN + KID, so the identification is his, not mine. mušīm šīmātim “who fixes the fates” (mušīm, the D participle of šâmum “to decide, fix”, Harper’s samu II,1; šīmātim the plural of šīmtum). ša kibīssu lā uttakkaru “whose command is not altered”: kibītum “speech, command” + -šu, the ssu written with ZU (Harper’s ki-be-zu), and uttakkaru the passive of the D of nakārum with the -u of the relative clause (Harper’s nakaru II,2, ut-ta-ka-ru). mušarbû šarrūtīya “who makes my kingship great”: the Š participle of rabûm (Harper’s rabu III,1 “to enlarge, make great”), šarrūtīya “my kingship”. All of this is description; the wishes follow in the next lines.

sentences.l: revolt not to-be-controlled(?), his-hand a-curse(?), his-perishing, in his-dwelling let-him-scatter for-him,
sentences.i: A revolt that cannot be put down (?), his hand, a curse (?), his ruin: in his dwelling may he scatter them for him,
sentences.n: Hard lines, which I read only as far as the words allow. tēši lā šubbîm: tēšû (Harper’s tešu “revolt”, te-ši) + lā + šubbîm, which Harper files under šabu II,1 “to attack, to control” (šu-ub-bi-im): “a revolt not to be controlled (?)”. qāssu raḫ: qāssu is qātum “hand” + -šu, the ss written with ZU (Harper’s ga-zu = qāssu); raḫ is listed by Harper as “curse” (his raḫlu): “his hand, a curse (?)”. ḫalāqišu “his perishing, his ruin” (the infinitive ḫalāqum + -šu); ina šubtišu “in his dwelling” (šubtum “dwelling” + -šu). lišappiḫaššum (Harper’s li-ša-ab-bi-ḫa-aš-šum) is li- + the D of sapāḫum “to scatter, to drive out” + -šum “for him”, “let him scatter for him”. How the pieces fit is UNCERTAIN; the five lines divide as Harper’s ruled lines do (59 te-ši la šu-ub-bi-im, with the last two signs in a sub-row; 60 ga-zu ra-aḫ; 61; 62; 63 with ḫa-aš-šum in a sub-row).

sentences.l: a-reign of-sighing, days few, years of-famine, darkness without light, death of-a-glance of-the-eye,
sentences.i: A reign of sighing, few days, years of famine, darkness without light, death of a glance of the eye (?) —
sentences.n: A list of the god’s gifts to the cursed man, all in the accusative, governed by lišīmšum in the next unit (“may he decree them for him as his fate”). palê tanēḫim: palûm “reign” (the BAL sign, Harper’s palû) and tanēḫum “sighing” (Harper’s taneḫu; the genitive after palê). ūmī iṣūtim: ūmī is the sign UD “days” (ûmi in Harper’s print marks a Sumerogram), iṣūtim the feminine plural of Harper’s isu “small, few”, written i-zu-tim with ZU for ṣu: “few days”. šanāt ḫušaḫḫim: šanāt is the plural of šattum “year” before a genitive, ḫušaḫḫum “hunger, famine”. iklit lā nawārim: Harper’s eklitu “darkness” (written ik-li-it), then lā nawārim “of no light”. mūt nīṭil īnim: mūt is mūtum “death” (not mutum “husband”), nīṭil is Harper’s nitlu “look, staring”, īnim “of the eye”: literally “death of a look of the eye”; I keep it literal (a sudden death?), and the force is UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: as-fate let-him-decree for-him.
sentences.i: may he decree them for him as his fate.
sentences.n: ana šīmtim lišīmšum: ana šīmtim “as a fate, for his fate” (as in the earlier parts, e.g. ana šīmtim ittalku), and lišīmšum is li- + išīm, the preterite of šâmum “to decide, to decree” (Harper’s samu I,1, li-ši-im-šum; the same verb as mušīm at xlii 54), + -šum “for him”. The objects, in the accusative, are the five things of the unit before.

sentences.l: the-perishing of-his-city, the-scattering of-his-people, his-kingship the-carrying-off(?), his-name and his-mention in the-land the-not-causing-to-be,
sentences.i: the ruin of his city, the scattering of his people, the carrying off (?) of his kingship, and that his name and his memory not be brought into being in the land —
sentences.n: More decrees, now as nouns in the construct, objects of liqbi in the next unit. ḫalāq ālišu “the perishing of his city” (ḫalāqum, with URU-šu “his city”); našpuḫ nišīšu “the scattering of his people” (našpuḫum, Harper’s sapahu IV,1, “to be dispersed”, the same root as lišappiḫaššum at xlii 63); šarrūssu šūbilam “the carrying off (?) of his kingship”: šarrūssu is šarrūtum + -šu (the ss written ZU), and šūbilam, Harper’s šu-bi-lam, which his glossary does enter, under his abalu (wabālum) III,1 “to bring, to take away, to transport” (with šu-bu-lu at xviii 60–61, 67); I read it as the Š-stem of wabālum “to carry”, with an accusative -am, “the carrying off”: UNCERTAIN (the vowels of šu-bi-lam are not those of the infinitive šūbulum, so the form may be something else). šumšu u zikiršu “his name and his mention” (zikrum “name, mention”, Harper’s zikru “name, vow”), ina mātim lā šubšâm “in the land, not to cause to be”: šubšâm is the Š infinitive of bašûm (Harper’s basu III,1, su-ub-sa-a-am) with lā: “not to bring into being”, that is, that no name or mention of him be brought forth in the land. The force follows the Š-stem (“to cause to be”); Harper gives no sense for the form.

sentences.l: with-his-mouth weighty let-him-say.
sentences.i: may he speak all this with his weighty mouth.
sentences.n: ina pīšu kabtim liqbi: pīšu is KA “mouth” + -šu “his” (Harper’s pî “mouth, command”), kabtim “heavy, mighty” (kabtum), and liqbi the precative of qabûm “to say” (Harper’s qibu I,1, li-iq-bi). It is the verb for everything listed from xlii 73: the god is to say these things with his weighty mouth, that is, to pronounce them. Plate 78 shows two separate ruled rows here, 79 (i-na pî-šu kab-tim, with the numeral 80 on the next row) and 80 (li-iq-bi), and the plate’s numerals (80, 85, 90, 95) fall on the rows the division gives them.

sentences.l: Bēlit, the-mother great, whose-command in Ekur is-weighty, the-lady who-makes-favorable my-igirrû(?),
sentences.i: Bēlit, the great mother, whose command is weighty in Ekur, the lady who makes my igirrû (plans? dreams?) favorable —
sentences.n: A goddess is called on, as the god was. Harper prints Bêlit, “the lady”, which here is a sign group with the star: {d}NIN.LÍL (the star, NIN and KID; Harper’s glossary gives BELIT [NIN.LIL], “goddess, consort of Bel”, at xlii 81, so the group is his own identification, and on the plate the last sign is the KID of Ellil’s name at xlii 53 and 89 and the sign before it looks like the one that begins bēltum at xlii 85; modern books call her Ninlil, and Bēlit is Harper’s reading of the name). ummum rabītum “the great mother”: ummum is the single sign AMA (Harper’s sign list no. 102, ummu “mother”) and rabītum the feminine of rabûm “great” (Harper’s ra-bi-tum). ša kibīssa ina Ekur kabtat “whose command is weighty in Ekur”: kibītum + -ša (the ss written ZA, Harper’s ki-be-za), É.KUR the temple Ekur, kabtat the stative of kabātum “to be heavy, to be potent” (Harper’s kabatu I,1). bēltum mudammiqat igirrīya: bēltum is the sign NIN “lady” (Harper’s bēltu “mistress, lady”); mudammiqat is the feminine D participle of damāqum, “who makes good, who favors” (Harper’s damaku II,1, mu-dam-mi-ga-at, with GA read qa₂); igirrīya is Harper’s egirru “dreams, plans” + -ia, as at xli 52, where the sense is unclear; UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: in-the-place-of judgment and decision, before Ellil, his-word let-her-make-evil,
sentences.i: in the place of judgment and decision, before Ellil, may she turn his word to evil,
sentences.n: The wish itself. ašar šipṭim ù purussîm: ašar “place (of)” before a genitive, šipṭim the genitive of šipṭum “judgment” (Harper’s šiptu, written ši-ip-di-im with DI for ṭi), purussîm the genitive of purussûm “decision”: “in the place of judgment and decision”. ina maḫar Ellil “before Ellil” ({d}EN.LÍL, Harper’s Bêl, as at xlii 53). awāssu is awātum “word, matter” + -šu (the ss written ZU, Harper’s a-wa-zu): “his word”. lilemmin is li- + the D of lemēnum “to be evil” (Harper’s limenu II,1, “to be evil, hostile”), “let her make evil”: let her turn his word, his case, against him, in the place where cases are judged. The subject is the goddess of the unit before.

sentences.l: the-overthrow of-his-land, the-perishing of-his-people, the-pouring-out of-his-life like water, by-the-mouth of-Ellil the-king let-her-cause-to-be-set.
sentences.i: may she have the overthrow of his land, the perishing of his people, the pouring out of his life like water set on him, at the command of Ellil the king.
sentences.n: The curse closes with three more nouns in the construct, the objects of the verb at the end. šulpūt mātišu “the overthrow of his land” (šulputum, Harper’s lapatu III,1 “to smite, overturn”); ḫalāq nišīšu “the perishing of his people”; tabāk napištišu “the pouring out of his life” (tabākum “to pour out”, napištum “life”; the sign Harper reads piš is his sign list no. 134, kir/piš, the GÍR sign, so the word is spelt na-GÍR-ti-šu); kīma mê “like water”. ina pî Ellil šarrim “at the mouth, by the command, of Ellil the king”: KA is pî, {d}EN.LÍL is Ellil, and šarrim is “of the king” in apposition (a name is not inflected, so the genitive shows on the title). lišaškin is li- + the Š of šakānum “to set”, “let her cause to be set”, the subject being the goddess of xlii 81, and “on him” being understood. The sentence ends here; the next god (Ea, written {d}EN.KI) is called on at xlii 98.
